newsitem.title: CANADA: CNR sets 83 pct operating ratio for 1997.
newsitem.headline: CNR sets 83 pct operating ratio for 1997.

text.p: Canadian National Railway Co said on Tuesday that it has set an operating ratio target of 83 percent for 1997, an improvement on the 85.3 percent ratio it realized in 1996.
"The target we are setting for ourselves in 1997 is 83 percent," CN President and Chief Executive Paul Tellier told Reuters in an interview.

Operating ratio measures operating expenses, net of financing charges, as a percentage of revenues. Analysts say it is a standard for evaluating a railroad's overall performance. The lower the ratio, the better the railway's performance.

Tellier said the average operating ratio for big U.S. railroads is about 80 percent, although some railways, such as Norfolk Southern Corp, can have ratios as low as 72 percent. CN's new operating ratio target for 1997 is "slightly lower" than the target set in its November 1995 initial public offering prospectus, he said.
"We are catching up, we are closing the gap, but we have got to do even better," Tellier said.
In the fourth quarter of 1996, CN's operating ratio dipped to 80.7 percent, but Tellier said it would be unrealistic to expect the railroad to maintain that ratio throughout 1997.

Tellier said he is expecting no further special charges relating to labor force reductions in 1997. In the fourth quarter of 1996, CN recorded a special charge of C$365 million relating to previously announced workforce reductions for 1996 and 1997.
"At this point in time, I don't forsee any other special charge in the forseeable future," Tellier said.
Tellier said that by December 31, 1997, CN expects to have about 20,000 permanent fulltime employees, down from just under 21,600 at year end 1996.
Tellier said the railroad will focus on revenue growth.
"We are confident that we can grow the revenues around the GDP rate in both countries, Canada and the United States," he said.

Tellier said he continues to talk with Canadian Pacific Ltd Chief Exeecutive William Stinson regarding a possible merger of the eastern operations of CN and CP unit Canadian Pacific Railway, but no definitive agreements are imminent.
Tellier said CN's eastern Canada operations were profitable for the first timme in the company's long history and he expects further progress this year.
Rather than a merger with CP Rail in eastern Canada or a buyout of CP's rail network there, CN would likely pursue a different approach to consolidating networks in that market, Tellier said.
"It is much more likely that what is going to come out of this is doing some discreet transactions here and there, proceeding on a more incremental basis," he said.
Tellier said that CN rationalized about 2,400 miles of track in 1996, beyond its 2,000-mile target, and that he expected further track rationalization of about 2,000 miles in 1997.
